title: Bank of Northlake - Security review (customer-managed KMS, rotation, audit logs)
summary: Bank of Northlake reviewed Redwood’s approach to customer-managed KMS for Private deployments, with emphasis on rotation cadence (scheduled + emergency), evidence/audit logging for key lifecycle events, and operational behavior during KMS degradation/outages. Redwood clarified envelope encryption (KEK/DEK), key version pinning, dual-read rotation window (new key first then bounded fallback), breakglass process, and what “rotation complete” means (data re-encrypted vs ability to decrypt old artifacts). Customer requested written rotation procedure, audit event list/schema, retention expectations, and failure-mode test expectations (timeouts, throttling, AccessDenied, disabled keys, regional outage). Call ended with concrete next steps for exchanging documents and scheduling a follow-up technical session focused on AWS KMS policy templates and installer preflight checks for Private.

transcript:
Meeting: Bank of Northlake - Security review (customer-managed KMS, rotation, audit logs)
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Date: 2026-01-14
Start time: 9:00 AM PT (approx)
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees (Redwood Inference): Simran Kaur, Marcus Lin, Olga Petrov, Elliot Price
Attendees (Bank of Northlake): Karen Holt, Miguel Alvarez, Priya Desai, Samir Qureshi

Auto Summary (generated):
- Discussed customer-managed KMS expectations for Private deployments.
- Clarified key rotation cadence and operational procedure (scheduled/emergency).
- Reviewed audit logging and evidence needs for regulated audits.
- Covered failure modes and expected behavior during KMS brownouts/outages.

Action items (generated):
- Redwood to share rotation procedure + audit event list.
- Bank to confirm rotation cadence and region constraints.

Transcript:

[00:00] Simran Kaur: Alright, good morning everyone. I’m Simran, I work on enterprise reference architectures here at Redwood Inference. I’ve got Marcus from Security Engineering, Olga from GRC, and Elliot from docs. Um, thanks for making the time.

[00:14] Karen Holt: Morning. Karen Holt, CISO. Thanks, Simran.

[00:18] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel, security architect. I’m the one with the KMS questions.

[00:21] Priya Desai: Priya, compliance and GRC.

[00:24] Samir Qureshi: Samir, platform engineering.

[00:27] Simran Kaur: Great. Goal today is to walk through how we do customer-managed keys, especially for Private deployments, and then make sure we can supply the written procedure and evidence you need. We can spend most of the time on KMS rotation, audit logs, and what happens during failures.

[00:45] Karen Holt: That’s exactly it. We’ve been through Bedrock and Azure OpenAI reviews, and the sticking points are always: who controls the key, what’s the rotation story, and what happens when KMS is down.

[00:56] Simran Kaur: Makes sense.

[01:00] Miguel Alvarez: I’ll start with the blunt version. For Private, we want customer-managed KMS. We want to be able to rotate on, call it, 90 days. We want evidence that it rotated. And we need to know you don’t brick the platform if AWS KMS has a bad day.

[01:17] Simran Kaur: Yep. All reasonable.

[01:19] Marcus Lin: I can take the “how keys are used” part. Then Olga can cover evidence, and we can circle back to the operational rotation mechanics.

[01:28] Simran Kaur: Go for it.

[01:30] Marcus Lin: So, across Hosted/Dedicated/Private we use envelope encryption patterns. Practically: we use a KEK in KMS to wrap a data encryption key, the DEK. The DEK is what actually encrypts the artifacts—think secrets, connection tokens, certain configuration blobs. The KEK stays in KMS.

[01:51] Miguel Alvarez: When you say “artifacts,” are we talking prompts? Or model outputs? Or…

[01:56] Simran Kaur: Good question. For Private, by default we’re not storing prompts or outputs unless you configure logging/retention features. The stuff we encrypt is platform operational data—credentials, integration secrets, some persisted state for the control plane. The exact set we can enumerate in the security appendix.

[02:15] Marcus Lin: And the key point: KMS calls are not on every token. This is not in the hot path per token. It’s for decrypting those encrypted blobs when needed.

[02:24] Samir Qureshi: So not per request to the model runtime.

[02:27] Marcus Lin: Correct. We do caching of decrypted DEKs in memory with TTLs, and we’re careful about minimizing KMS round trips.

[02:36] Miguel Alvarez: TTL as in, you keep the plaintext DEK in memory.

[02:39] Marcus Lin: In memory only, yes. With strict TTL, and we can tune it. There’s a tradeoff between KMS dependency and exposure window in memory.

[02:49] Karen Holt: We’ll want to understand the default TTL and whether we can set it.

[02:53] Simran Kaur: You can. In Private you have more knobs. Hosted is more fixed.

[03:00] Priya Desai: Before we get too deep: can you say clearly who “owns” the key in Private? Like, is it our AWS account and our KMS key? Or is it your account with a grant?

[03:10] Simran Kaur: In Private, typically it’s your AWS account, your key. Redwood services running in your environment are configured to use that key, with IAM permissions you control. We provide templates and guidance for least privilege.

[03:25] Miguel Alvarez: Is it multi-tenant inside our environment? I assume it’s dedicated to us.

[03:29] Simran Kaur: Private is single-tenant. Dedicated is also isolated capacity but hosted by us. Private is in your VPC or on-prem.

[03:39] Karen Holt: Okay. Rotation.

[03:41] Simran Kaur: Let’s do rotation. The mechanics we recommend: scheduled rotation—like every 90 days—is a planned workflow. Emergency rotation is “key might be compromised” and we need to cut over quickly.

[03:55] Miguel Alvarez: Right, and we need both.

[03:57] Simran Kaur: For both, we implement a dual-read window. During that window, decrypt tries the new key first and then falls back to the old key, but bounded—so we don’t keep old forever. This keeps downtime low.

[04:11] Samir Qureshi: Wait, AWS KMS rotation is “automatic” though, if you enable it. What are you rotating? Key ID or key version?

[04:18] Marcus Lin: Great catch. There are two layers. AWS-managed key material rotation changes the backing key material version inside KMS. That is transparent to callers. But customers often want a new CMK (new key ID/ARN) for policy reasons—like breaking glass or reducing blast radius. Our process supports changing which key ARN we use.

[04:40] Miguel Alvarez: We want new key ID. Not just the backing version.

[04:43] Marcus Lin: Understood. So our control plane config supports deterministic key selection and pinning. Meaning: you can pin to a specific key ARN (and where applicable key version semantics) so rollouts don’t accidentally drift.

[04:58] Karen Holt: “Where applicable” sounds like provider differences.

[05:02] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Azure Key Vault and GCP KMS have slightly different versioning APIs. AWS is mostly key ARN plus the KMS-managed rotation within it. But the high-level is: we can pin the configured key reference.

[05:16] Miguel Alvarez: Define “rotation complete.” This is one of those terms that always gets messy.

[05:21] Simran Kaur: Yes. We’re aligning on a clear definition.

[05:24] Marcus Lin: In our terminology, there’s (A) “cutover complete” meaning new encrypt operations use the new key, and decrypt operations can read both old and new during a transition. And (B) “re-encryption complete” meaning all stored ciphertexts that were encrypted under the old key have been rewrapped or re-encrypted so old key is no longer needed.

[05:46] Priya Desai: For audits, we’ll likely need B eventually.

[05:49] Marcus Lin: And that depends on data type. Some things can be rewrapped in place. Some are rotated as they’re touched. For Private we can run a background job to re-encrypt eligible artifacts, with progress and logs.

[06:06] Samir Qureshi: Is there a blocking migration? Like we rotate and then have to wait hours.

[06:11] Simran Kaur: No hard downtime requirement. The design is to avoid that. The dual-read window keeps it online.

[06:18] Miguel Alvarez: And if we disable the old key too early?

[06:21] Marcus Lin: Then any remaining ciphertext under the old key will fail to decrypt, and you’ll see errors. We provide a validation checklist and we recommend a staged approach: cutover, observe, run re-encryption, validate metrics, then disable.

[06:39] Karen Holt: We need this written. Like step-by-step with checklists.

[06:42] Elliot Price: Yep. We have an operator procedure doc specifically for Private. It includes prerequisites (IAM policy statements, key policy gotchas), a rotation workflow, and a troubleshooting section. We can share a version appropriate for customers.

[06:58] Priya Desai: Also: evidence. What do we get as a customer? Logs, events, etc.

[07:04] Olga Petrov: I can cover audit logging. We emit structured audit events for key lifecycle and KMS operations. Examples: configuration changes to key reference, rotation start/complete markers, decrypt failures with reason codes (like AccessDenied vs throttling), and key disablement detection.

[07:23] Miguel Alvarez: Do those include key IDs? Because we need to prove which key was used.

[07:27] Olga Petrov: We include the key identifier in a sanitized form. For Private, since it’s your environment, you can choose full ARN in your logs if you prefer, but we generally avoid leaking full resource identifiers in shared multi-tenant contexts. In Private it’s less sensitive, but we still keep the schema consistent.

[07:47] Samir Qureshi: Where do those events go? CloudWatch? Your system?

[07:52] Simran Kaur: In Private, you can route audit events to your SIEM—CloudWatch, Splunk, whatever you use. We ship a default pipeline, and you can integrate.

[08:02] Priya Desai: Retention. We need one year online, seven years archive is ideal. What do you support?

[08:09] Olga Petrov: For Private, retention is mainly your responsibility because the logs live in your account and your log retention policy. Redwood can provide guidance and a recommended baseline. For Hosted, we have default retention tiers.

[08:26] Karen Holt: Okay. Let’s talk failure modes.

[08:29] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah. What happens if KMS is throttling? Or regional outage? We’ve seen partial brownouts.

[08:36] Marcus Lin: We design for those. We have retry and backoff with jitter, plus a circuit breaker in the KMS client. We monitor latency, error codes, and breaker open state.

[08:49] Samir Qureshi: Circuit breaker means you stop calling KMS for a while.

[08:52] Marcus Lin: Right. If KMS is failing consistently, continuously retrying can amplify the problem and also can block threads. So breaker opens and we rely on cached DEKs where possible. If cache misses occur while KMS is unavailable, those operations may fail, but we try to scope impact and provide clear errors.

[09:12] Miguel Alvarez: “May fail” is scary. Which operations fail?

[09:15] Simran Kaur: Usually it’s things that require decrypting a secret that isn’t already cached—like a fresh startup of a service component, or first-time use of an integration token.

[09:26] Marcus Lin: Also: we’re not claiming we can operate indefinitely without KMS. It’s a dependency. The goal is graceful degradation and clear runbooks.

[09:37] Karen Holt: And your runbook includes what? Like “increase TTL.”

[09:41] Marcus Lin: Exactly. There are safe toggles: temporarily increase DEK cache TTL to reduce KMS calls; adjust breaker thresholds; and, in extreme cases, pause certain background jobs that would cause more KMS traffic.

[09:55] Samir Qureshi: But increasing TTL increases exposure if memory is compromised.

[09:59] Marcus Lin: Correct. That’s why it’s a temporary mitigation with approvals. Tradeoff is availability vs security exposure window.

[10:10] Priya Desai: Are those mitigations logged? If someone changes TTL or opens up access, we need an audit trail.

[10:17] Olga Petrov: Yes. Configuration changes and breakglass actions are auditable events.

[10:23] Karen Holt: Breakglass. Explain.

[10:25] Simran Kaur: For Private, breakglass is typically within your team because it’s your AWS account. But if Redwood is operating portions (depending on the support model), there’s a time-boxed, approval-based process to use elevated access, with post-incident review.

[10:43] Miguel Alvarez: We need to know you’re not holding a master key to our environment.

[10:47] Simran Kaur: Understood. The default is we do not have unilateral access to your CMK. You control the key policy. If you choose a support model where Redwood can assist, that would be an explicit, logged and scoped permission, and you can revoke it.

[11:06] Karen Holt: Okay.

[11:08] Miguel Alvarez: Let’s get specific. AWS KMS key policy. We’ve seen vendors say “just add *” and it becomes messy.

[11:14] Marcus Lin: We will not suggest star policies. Least privilege: the service role needs kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, and DescribeKey. For rotation and validation workflows you may need ListAliases depending on how you reference keys. We also recommend conditions on encryption context where possible.

[11:36] Samir Qureshi: Encryption context—are you using it?

[11:39] Marcus Lin: For certain objects yes, we can bind the ciphertext to a context including tenant/environment identifiers. It helps prevent swapping attacks, but also you need consistent context values across decrypt.

[11:53] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. But please document it. It can also cause weird failures when someone changes environment name.

[12:00] Simran Kaur: Totally. We’ll document the stable identifiers.

[12:06] Priya Desai: How do you test these failure modes? We want to see you’ve actually simulated KMS outage, not just “we have retries.”

[12:14] Marcus Lin: We run failure-mode tests in staging and do game days. We simulate timeouts, throttling, AccessDenied, disabled key, and sometimes region/API outage conditions using failure injection hooks.

[12:29] Karen Holt: Game day as in… you deliberately break KMS.

[12:32] Marcus Lin: In a controlled environment, yes.

[12:35] Samir Qureshi: And what are acceptance criteria? Like services keep running for N minutes?

[12:40] Simran Kaur: More like: for a given scenario, we define expected behavior—e.g., “no increased error rate for steady-state traffic if cache is warm,” “clear alerts fire within X minutes,” and “runbook leads to mitigation.”

[12:55] Miguel Alvarez: Warm cache assumption is big.

[12:58] Marcus Lin: We acknowledge that. That’s why we also test cold start under KMS impairment—what fails, how fast, and what message.

[13:08] Priya Desai: For regulatory, we also care about audit log completeness during failures.

[13:13] Olga Petrov: We’ll provide what we can. If KMS calls fail, we still emit an event that a decrypt failed and why, assuming the logging pipeline is up.

[13:25] Karen Holt: Okay. Rotation cadence. We said 90 days. Can you support 30 days? Some teams insist.

[13:31] Simran Kaur: Technically yes. But it increases operational overhead. The system is designed to make it low-downtime, but you still need to run the procedure and confirm re-encryption completeness if you’re changing key IDs.

[13:45] Miguel Alvarez: If we use AWS automatic rotation (key material) at 30 days, and key ID change at 90 days, would that work?

[13:52] Marcus Lin: That’s a common approach. Material rotation is seamless. Key ID change is the more involved one. We can support that.

[14:04] Samir Qureshi: How do you prevent drift—like some component still using the old key.

[14:09] Marcus Lin: That’s where deterministic key selection and config validation come in. The control plane config is versioned, validated, and can be pinned. We also have a health summary that can tell you which key reference is active for a tenant/environment.

[14:26] Miguel Alvarez: Health summary endpoint—does it leak sensitive info.

[14:29] Simran Kaur: It’s gated behind admin permissions and is sanitized. In Private you can scope it to your operators.

[14:36] Karen Holt: Okay, but we need to see it in writing.

[14:39] Elliot Price: Yep, we’ll include screenshots/examples. Redacted.

[14:44] Priya Desai: Audit events. Can you list them now? At least categories.

[14:49] Olga Petrov: Sure, categories: 
1) Key configuration changes (new key reference set, old key reference removed),
2) Rotation workflow events (rotation initiated, cutover completed, re-encryption job started/completed, validation passed/failed),
3) KMS operation events (encrypt/decrypt attempts with success/failure and error type),
4) Policy denials and IAM errors (AccessDenied, InvalidGrant, NotFound),
5) Key state changes observed (key disabled/scheduled deletion).

[15:24] Miguel Alvarez: Do you log plaintext? Please say no.

[15:26] Olga Petrov: No. No plaintext secrets in audit events.

[15:30] Karen Holt: Alright.

[15:32] Samir Qureshi: For Private installer—how do we know at install time we didn’t misconfigure IAM and then it fails later.

[15:40] Simran Kaur: We added preflight checks in the installer and upgrade flow. It validates it can reach KMS in the configured region, validates key is enabled, and checks required permissions by doing safe calls.

[15:55] Miguel Alvarez: That’s important. Some vendors only find out at runtime.

[15:59] Marcus Lin: And we also call out IAM propagation delays. Sometimes you attach policy and it’s not effective for a few minutes.

[16:07] Samir Qureshi: Yep, we’ve seen that.

[16:10] Karen Holt: On outages—do you have an SLA for KMS, like you’ll run multi-region.

[16:16] Simran Kaur: For Private, it depends on your architecture. If you want multi-region resiliency, we can support multi-region deployment patterns, but the KMS dependency follows your region choices. Some customers use multi-region keys. We can discuss options.

[16:33] Miguel Alvarez: We’re mostly us-east-1 and us-west-2. Regulators sometimes ask for data residency and DR.

[16:40] Simran Kaur: Got it.

[16:42] Priya Desai: You mentioned shared responsibility. Please articulate: what are we responsible for versus you.

[16:48] Simran Kaur: In Private: you own the AWS account, networking, KMS key, IAM policies, log retention, and access controls. Redwood provides the software, recommended configs, validation checks, and we can provide support. If you choose a managed operations model, we define which roles we assume and how it’s audited.

[17:12] Karen Holt: And for the key policy itself, we want to ensure Redwood can’t change it.

[17:16] Marcus Lin: Correct. Key policy changes are under your IAM governance.

[17:21] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. Let’s talk about “emergency rotation.” If we suspect compromise, what happens, step-by-step.

[17:29] Marcus Lin: Emergency rotation: you create a new CMK (or select one), update the configured key reference, then we enter a short dual-read window to preserve availability. You optionally run the re-encryption job with higher priority. Then you disable old key when validation indicates no remaining dependencies. In emergency mode, the window can be shorter, but risk is you disable too early.

[17:55] Karen Holt: Who flips the config? Us or you.

[17:57] Simran Kaur: In Private, you do. Or if you want Redwood assistance, we do it with your approval via breakglass process.

[18:06] Priya Desai: We’d want the emergency procedure to include communications: who gets paged, who signs off.

[18:12] Olga Petrov: We can include that as recommended governance.

[18:16] Samir Qureshi: The dual-read fallback—how long is bounded.

[18:21] Marcus Lin: Default might be hours to a couple days depending on artifact types, but it’s configurable. And we emit metrics so you can see if old-key decrypts are still happening.

[18:34] Miguel Alvarez: Metrics. What exactly.

[18:36] Marcus Lin: KMS latency, error rate by code, cache hit rate for DEKs, circuit breaker open count/time, and decrypt attempts by key reference (new vs old). Also per-tenant impact summaries.

[18:54] Karen Holt: Alerts—do you page on KMS latency or only on failures.

[18:58] Simran Kaur: We recommend paging on sustained elevated failure rates and breaker open state. Latency alerts can be noisy. Allison on our team is tuning thresholds; we can share recommendations.

[19:12] Miguel Alvarez: We want to avoid alert fatigue but also catch brownouts early. KMS throttling tends to show as increased latency first.

[19:20] Marcus Lin: Exactly. We can do multi-window alerting—warning on latency, page on failure + breaker.

[19:29] Priya Desai: For evidence, can we get a sample audit event payload.

[19:33] Olga Petrov: Yes, we’ll send a redacted example showing fields: timestamp, environment, operation type, key reference hash/ARN depending, result, error code, and correlation id.

[19:50] Karen Holt: Okay.

[19:52] Simran Kaur: Let me pause—anything else you want to cover that would block next step.

[19:57] Miguel Alvarez: I want to confirm: you can do “customer-managed KMS” without Redwood having to access the key in their AWS account. It’s in our account. And you support both types of rotation.

[20:07] Simran Kaur: Correct.

[20:09] Miguel Alvarez: And you have runbooks and you test failures.

[20:12] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[20:14] Karen Holt: We also need to know this is backwards compatible. Like we rotate and old ciphertext still can be read during the window.

[20:22] Marcus Lin: Yes, that’s the point of dual-read. And we are explicit about backwards compatibility guarantees. Old ciphertext remains decryptable with old key until you retire it.

[20:33] Samir Qureshi: Unless we disable it.

[20:35] Marcus Lin: Unless you disable it, yes.

[20:38] Karen Holt: Okay.

[20:40] Priya Desai: One more compliance item: if decrypt fails, does that get logged as an audit event.

[20:46] Olga Petrov: Yes, decrypt failure is an audit event with cause.

[20:50] Priya Desai: Good.

[20:52] Simran Kaur: Maybe helpful to talk about competitors quickly—because you mentioned Bedrock and Azure. Our main difference in Private is we can run the control plane and data plane in your environment. The security posture is closer to “your infra, your keys,” not a shared managed endpoint.

[21:10] Karen Holt: Understood.

[21:12] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. What do you need from us.

[21:15] Simran Kaur: Two things: your required rotation cadence and whether you require multi-region keys. Also any wording requirements for the security questionnaire—like whether you want us to say “customer exclusively controls the key.”

[21:30] Karen Holt: We’ll provide that. I’ll ask legal to weigh in too.

[21:36] Samir Qureshi: For the technical deep dive, I’d like someone who can talk through the exact AWS IAM policy statements and also the installer preflight. Because we’ve been burned by weird KMS endpoint settings.

[21:48] Simran Kaur: Marcus can do that, and I can bring Bruno Silva from our Private automation team if needed.

[21:56] Marcus Lin: Happy to.

[21:58] Miguel Alvarez: Also talk about encryption context and what identifiers you use. That can be tricky.

[22:04] Marcus Lin: Yep.

[22:06] Karen Holt: Time check. Let’s do recap and next steps.

[22:10] Simran Kaur: Sure. I’ll recap:
1) Private: customer-managed AWS KMS supported (key in your account), envelope encryption KEK/DEK.
2) Rotation: supports scheduled + emergency key ID rotation with dual-read window; defined “cutover complete” vs “re-encryption complete.”
3) Audit/evidence: structured audit events for key lifecycle, failures, and config changes; export to your SIEM; sample payloads and schema to be shared.
4) Resilience: caching + retry/backoff + circuit breaker; tested failure modes; runbooks with safe mitigations.

[22:43] Priya Desai: And deliverables are written docs.

[22:46] Simran Kaur: Yes. Next steps:
- We’ll send you the Private KMS rotation procedure doc and an audit event list/schema by Friday.
- We’ll schedule a 60-minute technical session early next week focusing on AWS KMS policy templates, encryption context, and installer preflight checks.
- You’ll confirm rotation requirements (90/30 days, key ID vs material) and region constraints (us-east-1/us-west-2, multi-region keys).

[23:12] Karen Holt: That works.

[23:14] Miguel Alvarez: Works. Please include failure mode expectations in the doc too. Like, what breaks first.

[23:20] Elliot Price: Noted. We’ll add a “known behavior during KMS degradation” section.

[23:25] Olga Petrov: And I’ll include an evidence mapping note: which audit events map to which control objectives.

[23:33] Karen Holt: Great. Thank you.

[23:36] Simran Kaur: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up with links and the invite.

[23:41] (Crosstalk)

[23:43] Samir Qureshi: Bye.

[23:44] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks.

[23:45] Karen Holt: Thanks.

[23:46] Call ended.

Note: Transcript may be truncated; Fireflies sometimes ends early if the meeting ended abruptly or audio dropped.
